title: Re-emerging Marburg virus disease in Africa: spillover ecology, geographic expansion, and surveillance vulnerabilities.
abstract: Marburg virus disease (MVD) is re-emerging across Africa as a high-consequence zoonosis shaped by expanding ecological suitability, repeated spillover, and uneven surveillance capacity. This review synthesizes current evidence on the ecological, epidemiological, and operational determinants of contemporary Marburg virus (MARV) emergence. We conceptualize MVD as an ecological-emergence system produced by interactions among reservoir-host biology, environmental change, human exposure, health-system readiness, and mobility, rather than as a series of isolated outbreaks. Recent detections in multiple African regions indicate wider enzootic circulation than previously recognized and support repeated, reservoir-associated introductions from distributed ecological foci. Spillover risk is heightened where mining, land-use change, agricultural encroachment, settlement growth, climate-sensitive habitat disruption, and population movement increase contact with Egyptian rousette bats ( Rousettus aegyptiacus ) and contaminated roost environments. Following primary spillover, diagnostic delays, fragmented surveillance, limited laboratory decentralization, healthcare-associated transmission, and mobility-linked exposure can enable outbreak amplification and delayed recognition. Serological findings further suggest possible "shadow epidemiology," with unrecognized or mild MARV infections occurring outside confirmed outbreak chains. Critical preparedness gaps persist in ecological risk mapping, longitudinal reservoir surveillance, decentralized molecular diagnostics, genomic sequencing, data integration, and cross-border early warning. Future preparedness should move beyond reactive containment toward integrated One Health approach combining predictive ecological surveillance, rapid community-level detection, real-time genomics, infection prevention, risk communication, and regional coordination to identify spillover early and prevent human transmission.

title: Marburg virus disease: a comprehensive review
abstract: SUMMARY Marburg virus disease (MVD) is a highly fatal illness closely resembling Ebola disease, caused by either Marburg virus (MARV) or Ravn virus (RAVV). It typically begins with a sudden onset of high fever, headache, and malaise, followed by severe gastrointestinal symptoms, bleeding disorders, and, in the most severe cases, multi-organ failure. Case fatality rates vary widely, from 24% up to 90%. MARV and RAVV are zoonotic pathogens, with fruit bats recognized as the main reservoir. Human-to-human transmission generally occurs through direct exposure to infected bodily fluids. Historically, MVD outbreaks were primarily restricted to Central and Eastern Africa. In recent years, however, the disease has appeared in new regions: Ghana recorded its first cases in 2022, followed by concurrent outbreaks in Equatorial Guinea and Tanzania in 2023. Rwanda and Ethiopia experienced their debut outbreaks in 2024 and 2025, respectively, and another outbreak occurred in early 2025 in Tanzania. These incidents point to a troubling rise in annual MVD outbreaks and emphasize the ongoing risk of spillover from wildlife reservoirs and continued human-to-human transmission. Currently, there are no approved vaccines or antiviral treatments for MVD. Patient care focuses on supportive therapies, including aggressive fluid resuscitation, management of blood pressure and circulation, and intensive critical care. Nonetheless, promising countermeasures, such as monoclonal antibodies and antiviral drugs, are advancing through research and clinical trials. Experimental vaccines, particularly those based on viral-vector technologies, have demonstrated robust immune responses and are undergoing human testing. This review provides clinicians with the most recent knowledge of MVD, with a focus on epidemiological patterns, diagnostic procedures, clinical management, and the latest progress in developing medical countermeasures.

title: Discovering host-viral protein interactions in autophagy: A LIR discovery pipeline for identifying LC3-interacting region motifs in highly virulent viruses.
abstract: Hemorrhagic fever virus (HFV) infections are highly fatal, posing a significant global pandemic threat as they continue to emerge in new locations. HFVs and other highly virulent viruses (HVVs), such as Nipah virus, exploit host cell pathways, including the conserved host autophagy pathway, to promote viral replication. The Atg8/microtubule-associated protein 1 light chain 3 (LC3) proteins are necessary for autophagosome formation and maturation. Proteins interact with Atg8-family proteins through LC3-interacting region (LIR) motifs, which is a short linear motif (SLiM) found in intrinsically disordered regions of proteins. The presence of these motifs in viral components suggests they play a role in hijacking or evading the host autophagy pathway, yet the identification of functional LIR motifs in viral proteins remains limited. To address this gap, we developed the LIR Discovery Pipeline (LIR-DP) which integrates amino acid sequence pattern matching, with protein disorder prediction using IUPred3, and modeling with AlphaFold3. Using LIR-DP, we identified 43 putative LIR motifs in 166 proteins from 22 HVVs and predicted that 18 of these LIRs would be functional. In vitro and in cellulo laboratory experiments demonstrated that LIRs from the Marburg virus nucleoprotein, the Nipah virus phosphoprotein, the Ebola virus VP35, and the Rift Valley fever virus NSs protein bind to Atg8/LC3 family proteins. The aromatic amino acid in the first position of each LIR motif was found to be critical for these interactions. We provide evidence for the utility of the LIR-DP in identifying functional LIRs within HVV proteins which may provide valuable insight into the mechanism by which HVVs modulate the autophagy pathway during infection.

title: Frontline-worker infections as a marker of infection-prevention stress during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo
abstract: Abstract Objective To quantify the reported burden, temporal contribution, mortality and health-zone distribution of frontline-worker infections during the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and to examine contemporaneous infection-prevention-and-control (IPC) evidence. Methods We conducted a retrospective longitudinal analysis of DRC situation reports, the INRB-UMIE BDBV2026-Data repository, and WHO outbreak updates, per STROBE principles. National health-worker snapshots were reconstructed for 10 June-9 August 2026; detailed Ituri Province tables were analysed for 13 July-4 August. Crude case fatality among frontline and other confirmed cases was compared using risk ratios and a stratified Mantel-Haenszel odds ratio. Findings Nationally, health-worker infections rose from 16/676 confirmed cases (2.4%) on 10 June to 151/3,605 (4.2%) on 30 July, contributing 11.0% of newly accumulated cases in the first three weeks but only 2.2-2.6% thereafter. Reported case fatality was lower among health workers, nationally on 30 July (29.1% versus 44.7%; risk ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.51-0.84) and in Ituri on 4 August (30.7% versus 42.8%; RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.56-0.92; stratified odds ratio 0.59, 95% CI 0.41-0.85). Burden was spatially concentrated but heterogeneous across health zones. IPC reports documented low facility scorecards, recurrent high-risk exposures, and inconsistent worker denominators. Conclusion Frontline-worker infections formed a substantial, front-loaded epidemic component and a visible IPC-stress marker, but aggregate data cannot establish occupational incidence or place of acquisition. Lower reported mortality likely reflects earlier recognition or care access rather than lower severity. Standardized worker denominators and linked occupational surveillance should be incorporated into Ebola situation reporting. What was already known on this topic Previous Ebola and Marburg outbreaks have demonstrated substantial health-worker involvement, with infections linked to inadequate triage, insufficient personal protective equipment, exposure to patients with unrecognized infection and fragile health systems. Occupational burden is often concentrated early in epidemics, and infections among health workers can disable essential services, erode workforce confidence and signal weaknesses in infection prevention and control. However, routine outbreak reports rarely document health-worker trajectories in detail or link them systematically to IPC performance. What this paper adds Using reconciled longitudinal national and provincial snapshots and detailed personnel de premiere ligne (PPL) tables from Ituri Province, this paper quantifies the reported burden, mortality and health-zone distribution of frontline-worker infections during the 2026 BVD outbreak. It shows that frontline infections formed a substantial, front-loaded component of the epidemic and remained a visible marker of IPC stress, while crude case-fatality ratios among frontline workers were lower than among other confirmed cases. It demonstrates that available aggregate data cannot establish occupational incidence or place of acquisition, and argues that standardized worker denominators and linked occupational surveillance should be incorporated into Ebola situation reporting.

title: Field Investigation of the Bundibugyo Ebola Virus Disease (BDBV) Outbreak in Ituri Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo: Challenges, Strategies, and Priority Actions for Outbreak Control—An Outbreak Investigation Review
abstract: Background: The 2026 outbreak of Bundibugyo Ebola virus disease (BDBV) in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), centered in Ituri Province, represents the largest documented outbreak caused by Bundibugyo ebolavirus since its discovery in Uganda in 2007. The outbreak evolved within a complex humanitarian setting characterized by armed conflict, population displacement, mining-related migration, weak health systems, extensive population mobility, and an infodemic environment marked by misinformation and reduced public trust. We conducted a field investigation to assess epidemiological, operational, laboratory, infection prevention and control (IPC), community engagement, risk communication, and infodemic management challenges and identify priority interventions to strengthen outbreak control. Methods: A rapid field assessment was conducted between 12–15 June 2026 in Bunia, Rwampara Health Zone, and the Ituri Provincial Public Health Laboratory. Data were collected through direct observation, review of surveillance and laboratory reports, health facility assessments, stakeholder interviews, and analysis of outbreak response indicators. Epidemiological trends, surveillance performance, laboratory capacity, clinical care, IPC activities, logistics, risk communication, community engagement, and infodemic management approaches were evaluated. Results: As of 12 July 2026, the outbreak had resulted in 1926 laboratory-confirmed cases and 702 deaths, corresponding to an overall case fatality rate (CFR) of 36.4% across affected provinces. Ituri Province remained the epicenter, accounting for 90.8% of confirmed cases (1705/1877) and 85.5% of reported deaths (577/675). During the preceding 24 h, 53 new confirmed cases and 30 deaths were reported, including 20 community deaths (66.7%), highlighting persistent delays in detection, referral, and access to care. Surveillance systems identified 766 alerts, of which 678 (88.5%) were investigated, resulting in 235 suspected cases. Contact tracing remained a major challenge, with only 64.4% (4171/6475) of registered contacts successfully followed, below the recommended ≥95% target. Laboratory activities included testing of 137 specimens, with 29 positive results and an overall positivity rate of 21.2%. Decentralized molecular diagnostic platforms improved access to testing; however, data inconsistencies, delayed investigations, and gaps in outcome classification affected response monitoring. Major operational challenges included limited treatment capacity, high occupancy of Ebola treatment centres, shortages of trained personnel and IPC supplies, insecurity affecting response teams, and insufficient preparedness in newly affected areas. Community resistance, attacks on burial teams, detention of frontline responders, misinformation, and rumors contributed to delayed care-seeking, reduced acceptance of public health measures, and incomplete cooperation with contact tracing. Risk communication and community engagement efforts were constrained by limited outreach capacity, language barriers, low trust, and inadequate systems for rumor detection and infodemic response. Conclusions: The ongoing BDBV outbreak in eastern DRC demonstrates the difficulty of controlling Ebola transmission in conflict-affected and socially complex settings. Sustained transmission, community deaths, geographic expansion, and operational constraints highlight the urgent need to strengthen surveillance, contact tracing, laboratory systems, IPC capacity, clinical care, and integrated risk communication and infodemic management strategies. Building trust through community-centered approaches, proactive misinformation management, and engagement of trusted local actors will be essential to accelerate outbreak containment and strengthen preparedness across the Great Lakes region.

title: Ebola virus mRNAs contain RNA structures that are critical for viral infection and targetable by antisense oligonucleotides
abstract: Abstract Filoviruses, such as Ebola virus (EBOV), are highly pathogenic non-segmented negative-sense RNA viruses (nsNSVs) with limited therapeutic options. Filovirus RNA structures remain largely untapped due to the enhanced biosafety requirements for handling infectious virus. Here, we present the first in-cell secondary structure maps of four EBOV mRNAs (VP35, VP40, VP30, and VP24) using two orthogonal chemical probing approaches: SHAPE-MaP and fbDMS-MaP. We find that EBOV mRNA coding sequences (CDS) are highly structured, much like +ssRNA viruses, whereas untranslated regions (UTRs) are significantly less structured. This suggests that high CDS structure contents are general features of viral translation templates, and that nsNSVs have evolved separate regulatory function at the RNA structure level that extends beyond using distinct mRNAs and genomes. These structure maps are consistent with formation of mRNA 5′ hairpin structures during infection and reveal numerous additional RNA structures within the CDS, 3′ UTRs, and at CDS-UTR junctions. To assess functionality, we disrupted these structures with locked nucleic acid (LNA) antisense oligonucleotides. Disrupting the TSS hairpins in VP35, VP30, and VP24 decreased infection by >60%, indicating these mRNA structures are critical for infection. LNA targeting of the newly identified structures reduced EBOV infection by 31% to 88%, thereby linking RNA structural integrity to viral function. Synonymous mutation rates and covariation analysis provided evolutionary support across mammalian filoviruses for the functional RNA elements observed. Collectively, these results demonstrate EBOV mRNAs contain numerous conserved RNA motifs contributing to viral infection, and that these elements represent promising targets for development of pan-filoviral therapeutics. Importance EBOV and related filoviruses pose a significant global health threat, yet our understanding of the RNA architectural mechanisms driving infection remains incomplete. Due to enhanced biosafety constraints, filovirus RNA structures have not been mapped in cells. Here, we experimentally map secondary structures of four EBOV mRNAs at biosafety level 4. We find that structure content is concentrated within protein coding regions, resembling the highly structured genomes of positive-sense RNA viruses, while untranslated regions are relatively unstructured. This separation of relative structural content reflects how translation and replication are delegated between mRNAs and genomes in negative-sense RNA viruses. We also show that these structures are critical for infection, with disruption reducing infection more than 80% in liver cells. Evolutionary analyses suggest a set of these regulatory elements are conserved across mammalian filoviruses. Broadly, this work expands the repertoire of filovirus regulatory elements, revealing new potential targets for developing pan-filoviral therapeutics.

title: Allosteric remodelling of the Ebola virus glycoprotein underlies differences in entry mechanisms across species
abstract: Abstract During Ebola virus transit through the endo-lysosomal pathway, the glycoprotein GP undergoes a series of conformational rearrangements upon cathepsin cleavage and NPC1 receptor binding, culminating in host-virus membrane fusion. While these rearrangements underpin viral entry, their molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we combine hydrogen/deuterium-exchange mass spectrometry and mass photometry to resolve structural dynamic and energetic transitions of GP of two major species, Zaire (EBOV) and Sudan (SUDV). We describe the allosteric axes that govern reorganization of the cleavage sites, opening of the receptor binding cavity and priming for fusion upon NPC1 engagement. We show that GP cathepsin cleavage and receptor binding exhibit different mechanisms and kinetics across species, and are allosterically coupled in a species-specific manner. We reveal that fusion priming is optimized via distinct routes in EBOV and SUDV GP. These data suggest that GP structural dynamics and allosteric remodelling underlie differences in entry mechanisms across Ebolavirus species.

title: A Fractional-Order Nonlinear Model for The Transmission Dynamics of Ebola Virus Disease with Quarantine, Vaccination, and Condom Use
abstract: This paper presents a non-linear fractional-order mathematical model for the transmission dynamics of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD), incorporating key control measures such as quarantine, vaccination, and condom use. full_text: Abstract Background The 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), with cross-border cases in Uganda, evolved amid mobility, insecurity, delayed detection, laboratory constraints and pressure on case management. We assessed how official aggregate data with documented source provenance could support real-time description of reported case growth, outcome heterogeneity and response constraints. Methods We conducted a retrospective aggregate time-series and subnational ecological analysis of official situation reports and public health updates. The DRC analysis used national, provincial and health-zone data from situation reports 001– 028 covering 14 May–11 June 2026; Uganda was analysed separately through 10 June 2026. Outcomes included epidemic trajectory, growth of reported cumulative confirmed cases, crude observed case-fatality ratios (CFRs) and selected operational indicators. Growth estimates were treated as descriptive measures of reported case accumulation, not direct estimates of transmission intensity. Results Between 14 May and 11 June 2026, DRC recorded 689 confirmed cases and 139 confirmed deaths across 29 health zones, corresponding to a crude observed CFR of 20.2% (95% CI 17.2–23.4%). Ituri province accounted for 646 cases (93.8%) and had a CFR of 17.6% (95% CI 14.8–20.8%). By 10 June 2026, Uganda had recorded 19 confirmed cases and two confirmed deaths. In the DRC, apparent doubling times were similar during 21–27 May and 4–10 June 2026 (10.5 and 10.3 days, respectively), with a shorter estimate of 7.4 days during 28 May–3 June 2026. Among eligible Ituri health zones, CFRs ranged from 3.0% in Nyankunde to 38.2% in Mongbwalu. Contact follow-up reached 71.8% on 10 June. Ituri test positivity ranged from 26.6% to 68.5% across four reported time points. Conclusions Official aggregate data from DRC and Uganda during the early 2026 BVD outbreak showed continued accumulation of confirmed cases, geographic expansion, crude outcome heterogeneity and operational constraints in contact follow-up, case management and laboratory turnaround. Phase-specific growth estimates were sensitive to surveillance-series representation and should be interpreted primarily as descriptive measures of reported case accumulation, not direct transmission estimates. Transparent documentation of revisions, unresolved outcomes and subnational data gaps is essential for credible real-time outbreak analysis. full_text: Infektionen durch Ebolaviren zählen zu den schwerwiegendsten viralen Erkrankungen des Menschen [1]. Obwohl importierte oder evakuierte Fälle in Deutschland extrem selten sind, besitzt die Ebolaviruserkrankung aufgrund ihrer hohen Letalität, der erforderlichen Hochisolationsmaßnahmen und der raschen Entwicklung eines septischen Multiorganversagens erhebliche Bedeutung für die Intensiv- und Notfallmedizin. Eine frühzeitige Verdachtsdiagnose, konsequente Isolation und eine strukturierte intensivmedizinische Supportivtherapie sind entscheidend für das Überleben der Betroffenen und den Schutz des Personals. Ebolaviren Ebolaviren gehören zur Gattung Orthoebolavirus (Familie Filoviridae); es handelt sich um behüllte, filamentöse RNA-Viren mit negativsträngigem Genom [2]. Klinisch bedeutsam sind vor allem das Zaire-, das Sudan- und das Bundibugyo-Ebolavirus. Natürliches Reservoir sind Fruchtfledermäuse, von denen zoonotische Spillover-Ereignisse auf Primaten und den Menschen ausgehen können. Nach Aufnahme über das virale Glykoprotein und den intrazellulären NPC1-Rezeptor infiziert das Virus bevorzugt Monozyten, Makrophagen und dendritische Zellen; die viralen Proteine VP35 und VP24 hemmen die Typ-I-Interferon-Antwort und begünstigen hohe, prognostisch ungünstige Viruslasten [1, 3]. Pathophysiologie Die Organschäden beruhen weniger auf einer direkten zytopathischen Wirkung als auf einer ausgeprägten Dysregulation der Wirtsimmunantwort. Infizierte Monozyten und Makrophagen setzen große Mengen proinflammatorischer Zytokine frei (u. a. Interleukin‐6, Interleukin-1β und TNF-α). Der resultierende Zytokinsturm führt zu Endothelaktivierung, Verlust der Glykokalyx, erhöhter Gefäßpermeabilität und einem ausgeprägten Kapillarlecksyndrom [1, 3]. Gleichzeitig aktiviert die Expression von Tissue Factor auf Monozyten die Gerinnungskaskade und begünstigt Mikrothrombosierung sowie eine disseminierte intravasale Gerinnung [1]. Insgesamt ähnelt das Krankheitsbild einem hyperinflammatorischen septischen Schock mit ausgeprägter endothelialer Dysfunktion. Erhöhte Serumkonzentrationen von Angiopoetin‐2, Ferritin und Interleukin‐6 korrelieren mit der Erkrankungsschwere und eignen sich zur frühen Risikostratifizierung [3]. Klinik Die Inkubationszeit beträgt in der Regel 2–21 Tage [4]. Initial bestehen unspezifische Symptome wie hohes Fieber, ausgeprägte Abgeschlagenheit, Myalgien und Kopfschmerzen, weshalb insbesondere bei Reiserückkehrern aus Endemiegebieten eine sorgfältige epidemiologische Anamnese essenziell ist. Im weiteren Verlauf entwickeln viele Patientinnen und Patienten eine schwere gastrointestinale Symptomatik mit Erbrechen und profusen Diarrhöen; der Flüssigkeits- und Elektrolytverlust führt rasch zu Hypovolämie und hämodynamischer Instabilität [3, 5]. Schwere Verläufe sind durch septischen Schock, akutes Nierenversagen, Leberfunktionsstörungen, respiratorische Insuffizienz sowie neurologische Manifestationen gekennzeichnet; hämorrhagische Komplikationen treten seltener auf als früher angenommen, sind jedoch prognostisch ungünstig. Die Letalität liegt je nach Virusspezies und Versorgungsbedingungen zwischen 30 und 90 % [1, 4]. Differenzialdiagnostisch sind vor allem Malaria, bakterielle Sepsis, Typhus abdominalis sowie Lassa- und Marburgvirusinfektionen zu berücksichtigen. Überlebende entwickeln häufig ein Post-Ebola-Syndrom mit okulären, neurologischen und muskuloskeletalen Beschwerden [6]. Diagnostik Die Diagnose stützt sich auf die Kombination aus klinischer Symptomatik, epidemiologischer Expositionsanamnese und spezifischer virologischer Diagnostik. Goldstandard ist der Nachweis viraler RNA mittels RT-PCR aus Blutproben, der bereits in der Frühphase eine zuverlässige Diagnosesicherung ermöglicht [7, 8]. Typische Laborbefunde sind Thrombozytopenie, erhöhte Transaminasen, Gerinnungsstörungen, Laktaterhöhung, metabolische Azidose sowie ein Kreatininanstieg als Ausdruck einer beginnenden Multiorganbeteiligung ([8]; Abb. 1). Initiales Management bei HCID-Verdacht Bereits bei begründetem Verdacht auf eine hochkontagiöse Erkrankung („high consequence infectious disease“ [HCID]) ist ein standardisiertes Vorgehen entscheidend: frühzeitige Identifikation des epidemiologischen Risikos, sofortige räumliche Isolation, konsequente Verwendung persönlicher Schutzausrüstung, Information des Krankenhaushygieneteams sowie umgehende Kontaktaufnahme mit dem Gesundheitsamt und dem zuständigen STAKOB-Zentrum [6, 9]. Zur strukturierten Verdachtsabklärung dient das webbasierte HCID-Flowtool von RKI und STAKOB (https://multimedia.gsb.bund.de/RKI/Flowcharts/HCID-FS/#/), das klinische Symptome, epidemiologische Risikofaktoren und die erforderlichen Erstmaßnahmen abbildet. Erst danach folgen gezielte Diagnostik, Risikobewertung und gegebenenfalls die Verlegung in ein spezialisiertes Hochisolationszentrum. Dieses strukturierte Vorgehen reduziert das Risiko nosokomialer Übertragungen. Therapie Grundlage jeder Behandlung ist eine frühzeitige, optimierte Supportivtherapie, die die Überlebenschancen deutlich verbessert [4]. Im Vordergrund stehen die konsequente Korrektur des Flüssigkeits- und Elektrolytverlusts, die Überwachung von Blutzucker und Säure-Basen-Haushalt, ein hämodynamisches Monitoring mit frühzeitiger Vasopressortherapie, eine lungenprotektive Beatmung sowie Nierenersatzverfahren bei akutem Nierenversagen. Intramuskuläre Injektionen und NSAR sollten wegen des Blutungsrisikos vermieden werden; bei Koagulopathie können Blutprodukte (Thrombozyten‐, Frischplasma- und Erythrozytenkonzentrate) erforderlich werden [7]. Bakterielle Superinfektionen und eine Malaria müssen frühzeitig ausgeschlossen bzw. mitbehandelt werden. Extrakorporale Verfahren (va-/vv-ECMO) kommen allenfalls als Ultima Ratio bei therapierefraktärem kardiogenem Schock beziehungsweise nach erfolgloser Bauchlagerung in Betracht; ihr Einsatz bleibt auf spezialisierte Hochisolationszentren beschränkt und wird durch die hohen infektionshygienischen Anforderungen und das Expositionsrisiko für das Personal limitiert. Eine erregerspezifische Therapie steht bislang nur für das Zaire-Ebolavirus zur Verfügung: Die beiden monoklonalen Antikörper Ansuvimab (Ebanga®) und REGN-EB3 (Inmazeb®) führten in einer randomisierten, kontrollierten Studie zu einem deutlich besseren Überleben im Vergleich zur Kontrollgruppe und werden von der WHO frühzeitig empfohlen [10]. Beide sind in Deutschland nicht zugelassen und werden nach Expertenkonsultation als individueller Heilversuch angewandt [7]. Für die übrigen Ebolavirus-Spezies existiert bislang keine zugelassene Therapie; die Behandlung erfolgt in spezialisierten Zentren. Weitere Substanzen befinden sich in klinischer Prüfung. Remdesivir („off label“) und der experimentelle Antikörpercocktail MBP134 werden seit Juli 2026 in der WHO-koordinierten PARTNERS-Studie untersucht ([5, 7, 10]; Tab. 1; Abb. 1). Infektionsprävention Für medizinisches Personal hat der Eigenschutz höchste Priorität. Spezifische mAB-Präparate haben die Behandlung und Prognose bei Infektionen mit dem Zaire-Ebolavirus wesentlich verbessert. Obwohl importierte oder evakuierte Fälle in Deutschland extrem selten sind, besitzt die Ebolaviruserkrankung aufgrund ihrer hohen Letalität, der erforderlichen Hochisolationsmaßnahmen und der raschen Entwicklung eines septischen Multiorganversagens erhebliche Bedeutung für die Intensiv- und Notfallmedizin. Eine frühzeitige Verdachtsdiagnose, konsequente Isolation und eine strukturierte intensivmedizinische Supportivtherapie sind entscheidend für das Überleben der Betroffenen und den Schutz des Personals. Ebolaviren Ebolaviren gehören zur Gattung Orthoebolavirus (Familie Filoviridae); es handelt sich um behüllte, filamentöse RNA-Viren mit negativsträngigem Genom [2]. Klinisch bedeutsam sind vor allem das Zaire-, das Sudan- und das Bundibugyo-Ebolavirus. Natürliches Reservoir sind Fruchtfledermäuse, von denen zoonotische Spillover-Ereignisse auf Primaten und den Menschen ausgehen können. Nach Aufnahme über das virale Glykoprotein und den intrazellulären NPC1-Rezeptor infiziert das Virus bevorzugt Monozyten, Makrophagen und dendritische Zellen; die viralen Proteine VP35 und VP24 hemmen die Typ-I-Interferon-Antwort und begünstigen hohe, prognostisch ungünstige Viruslasten [1, 3]. Pathophysiologie Die Organschäden beruhen weniger auf einer direkten zytopathischen Wirkung als auf einer ausgeprägten Dysregulation der Wirtsimmunantwort. Gleichzeitig aktiviert die Expression von Tissue Factor auf Monozyten die Gerinnungskaskade und begünstigt Mikrothrombosierung sowie eine disseminierte intravasale Gerinnung [1]. Insgesamt ähnelt das Krankheitsbild einem hyperinflammatorischen septischen Schock mit ausgeprägter endothelialer Dysfunktion. Erhöhte Serumkonzentrationen von Angiopoetin‐2, Ferritin und Interleukin‐6 korrelieren mit der Erkrankungsschwere und eignen sich zur frühen Risikostratifizierung [3]. Klinik Die Inkubationszeit beträgt in der Regel 2–21 Tage [4]. Initial bestehen unspezifische Symptome wie hohes Fieber, ausgeprägte Abgeschlagenheit, Myalgien und Kopfschmerzen, weshalb insbesondere bei Reiserückkehrern aus Endemiegebieten eine sorgfältige epidemiologische Anamnese essenziell ist. Im weiteren Verlauf entwickeln viele Patientinnen und Patienten eine schwere gastrointestinale Symptomatik mit Erbrechen und profusen Diarrhöen; der Flüssigkeits- und Elektrolytverlust führt rasch zu Hypovolämie und hämodynamischer Instabilität [3, 5]. Schwere Verläufe sind durch septischen Schock, akutes Nierenversagen, Leberfunktionsstörungen, respiratorische Insuffizienz sowie neurologische Manifestationen gekennzeichnet; hämorrhagische Komplikationen treten seltener auf als früher angenommen, sind jedoch prognostisch ungünstig. Überlebende entwickeln häufig ein Post-Ebola-Syndrom mit okulären, neurologischen und muskuloskeletalen Beschwerden [6]. Diagnostik Die Diagnose stützt sich auf die Kombination aus klinischer Symptomatik, epidemiologischer Expositionsanamnese und spezifischer virologischer Diagnostik. Goldstandard ist der Nachweis viraler RNA mittels RT-PCR aus Blutproben, der bereits in der Frühphase eine zuverlässige Diagnosesicherung ermöglicht [7, 8]. Typische Laborbefunde sind Thrombozytopenie, erhöhte Transaminasen, Gerinnungsstörungen, Laktaterhöhung, metabolische Azidose sowie ein Kreatininanstieg als Ausdruck einer beginnenden Multiorganbeteiligung ([8]; Abb. 1). full_text: Abstract Nipah virus (NiV) is a highly pathogenic zoonotic RNA virus belonging to the genus Henipavirus within the family Paramyxoviridae, representing a continuing global health concern due to its high case fatality rate and potential for epidemic expansion in the era of increasing international connectivity. The virus demonstrates strong evolutionary adaptability driven by the absence of proofreading mechanisms during RNA replication, enabling genetic diversification that may influence host range, virulence, and transmission dynamics. Molecular pathogenesis of NiV is primarily mediated through interaction of viral glycoproteins with ephrin-B2 and ephrin-B3 receptors, facilitating host cell entry, endothelial damage, and neuroinvasion. Immune evasion facilitated by the action of accessory proteins encoded by the P gene (P, V, W, and C) acts to suppress innate antiviral immunity through the inhibition of interferon induction and JAK/STAT signaling. Human-to-human transmission of Nipah virus remains limited, with epidemiological evidence indicating basic reproduction numbers generally below unity; however, respiratory involvement and healthcare-associated exposure may enhance cluster outbreaks. Global travel, ecological disruption, and fragmented surveillance systems contribute to spillover risk, particularly in South and Southeast Asia where fruit bats of the genus Pteropus serve as natural reservoirs. Despite advances in vaccine technology, including subunit, viral vector, mRNA-based platforms, and monoclonal antibody therapies, no licensed prophylactic or therapeutic agent is currently available for human use. Global preparedness remains challenged by the scarcity of high-containment biosafety facilities, limited research funding, and absence of integrated One Health surveillance networks. Ethical considerations surrounding wildlife population control further complicate disease mitigation strategies. Emerging genomic surveillance, artificial intelligence–assisted predictive modeling, and regional data-sharing frameworks are essential for early detection and response. Strengthening molecular research on viral–host interactions and transmission determinants will be critical for preventing future Nipah virus outbreaks in an increasingly interconnected world. Graphical abstract Introduction Nipah virus (NiV) is an RNA virus that belongs to the family Paramyxoviridae. It is a member of the Henipavirus genus, which also comprises Hendra virus (HeV) and the newly discovered Cedar virus [1, 2]. NiV is a highly virulent Henipavirus that is mainly transmitted from fruit bats (of the genus Pteropus), its natural host, to humans either directly or through an intermediate host like pigs. NiV infections cause severe encephalitis and respiratory disease with case fatality rates ranging from 40 to 75% with no approved vaccines or antiviral therapies available [3]. The World Health Organization (WHO) has listed NiV as a priority pathogen because of its high mortality rate and potential for causing epidemics, and it recommends increased surveillance and preparedness [4]. Mutation potential RNA virus evolution Nipah virus (NiV), is an enveloped virus with a negative sense single-stranded RNA genome of helical symmetry. The nonsegmented, linear genome of Nipah virus is organized in the 3′ to 5′ direction and comprises six consecutively arranged genes that encode the nucleocapsid protein (N), phosphoprotein (P), matrix protein (M), fusion glycoprotein (F), attachment glycoprotein (G), and large polymerase (L) [5, 6] (Fig. 1). NiV being an RNA virus tends to have a higher rate of mutations compared to DNA viruses because RNA viruses do not have a proofreading mechanism during their replication. Because of the lack of proofreading ability during genome replication, the RNA virus NiV harbors evolutionary capacity. There is little information from genomic analysis supporting that natural mutation leads to any evolutionary change in either the range of host or its transmissibility or virulence in human cases. Hence, there is still a need for continued genome surveillance to look out for any such changes. The knowledge of this natural mutation ability is crucial in predicting the potential changes in the virulence, host range, and outbreak potential of the virus [7]. Genetic determinants of host interaction Attachment and entry mechanism The entry of NiV into host cells is mainly facilitated by its two surface glycoproteins, namely the G (attachment) glycoprotein and the F (fusion) glycoprotein. The G protein attaches with high affinity to the host cell surface receptors ephrin-B2 and ephrin-B3, which are highly conserved proteins among mammalian species. This attachment is crucial for the virus to attach to the host cell surface, and failure of the attachment process makes it impossible for the virus to enter the host cell. The conformational change that follows triggers the F glycoprotein to fuse the viral membrane with the host cell membrane, releasing the viral RNA into the cytoplasm for replication [8]. Structural basis and interactions Crystal structure analysis of the NiV-G glycoprotein in complex with ephrin-B2 or ephrin-B3 reveals that the viral protein interacts with the beta-propeller domain of these receptors through a defined protein–protein interface. This structural interaction defines the efficiency of viral attachment and infection. The shared binding interface for ephrin-B2 and ephrin-B3 enables NiV to infect a wide range of host cells, thus explaining the wide host tropism and high pathogenicity of NiV [9, 10]. Consequences of mutations on binding efficiency Mutational analysis and protein–protein interaction data suggest that certain residues within the host receptor and the viral glycoprotein can affect binding affinity and infection efficiency. For instance, mutations within the G-H loop of ephrin-B2 can modulate the binding affinity of NiV-G, thereby increasing or decreasing viral entry. Such modifications in binding efficiency can influence the viral infectivity and pathogenicity in various species [11]. Host tropism and computational predictions In silico analysis, such as protein–protein docking, has verified that NiV-G has stable interactions with ephrin-B2 and ephrin-B3 of various mammalian hosts, which implies that even small variations in the receptor sequences among species may affect host susceptibility. These models are valuable for predicting possible intermediate hosts and spillover susceptibility [12]. Therapeutic implications Given the importance of the G–ephrin interaction as an initial step in the NiV infection process, this interaction represents an attractive target for antiviral drugs and neutralizing antibodies. Inhibition of this interaction, either through the design of peptides that inhibit the binding of G to ephrin receptors or by locking the F protein in its prefusion state, could potentially inhibit viral entry and infection [13] (Fig. 2). These entry-associated mechanisms represent major targets for intervention and form the basis of several vaccine, monoclonal antibody, and antiviral strategies discussed in greater detail in the “Research Priorities” section of this review. Host immune evasion and pathogenesis of Nipah virus Nipah virus (NiV), classified as one of the highly pathogenic members of the Henipavirus genus, displays highly evolved immune evasion capabilities, as well as pathogenicity across multiple organ systems, mediated by interference with the host’s innate immune response, endothelial cell dysfunction, uncontrolled inflammation, and neuroinvasion. Interferon antagonism: the role of P gene products One of the hallmarks of NiV pathogenesis is the virus’s ability to downregulate the host innate immune response, which is mediated by the NiV P gene, which expresses multiple accessory proteins, including the P, V, W and C proteins, by RNA editing, which interfere with the host innate immune response by antagonizing both type I IFNs, including IFN-α/β, and type II IFNs, including IFN-γ, by interacting with key components of the JAK/STAT cascade, where the V and W proteins of NiV interact with both STAT1 and STAT2, inhibiting their phosphorylation, translocation, and activation of ISGs [14]. Significantly, it has been shown in studies on the ferret model that disruption of only the binding site for STAT1 is insufficient to eliminate virulence, as mutant viruses with mutations within the STAT1-interacting domains were found to be capable of causing lethal infection. Comparative analysis of V and W protein-deficient viruses also showed that each exhibited different pathogenic features, which implied that the C-terminal domains of these proteins might encode functions responsible for virulence that are independent of JAK/STAT signaling inhibition. The C protein, along with the well-known P, V, and W proteins, plays an important role in the efficiency of the virus by influencing the host’s response to the viral infection. W protein also localizes to the nucleus, which affects the host antiviral gene expression even more directly [15, 16]. The attenuation of viral virulence, following the deletion of these accessory proteins, has been clearly demonstrated by animal studies, which highlights their crucial importance for immune evasion and pathogenicity [17]. This potent antagonism of the host’s IFN response enables NiV to replicate efficiently during the early stages of infection, prior to the induction of the specific immune response (Fig. 3(1)). Cytokine dysregulation and “cytokine storm” potential The severe form of NiV infection is associated with significant immune activation and cytokine dysregulation. Studies have shown that proinflammatory cytokines, such as IL-6, TNF-alpha, MCP-1, and IP-10, are significantly elevated in the severe form of the disease, particularly in fatal cases of NiV infection [18]. The phenomenon of cytokine storm should be used judiciously to define the pathogenesis of viral infections, including NiV infection. However, it is apparent that immune system involvement in the pathogenesis of NiV infection is significant, as suggested by the “cytokine storm” in the context of NiV encephalitis [2]. The balance of immune defense and immunopathology may be critical in determining the outcome of the disease (Fig. 3(2)). Endothelial damage and vasculitis One of the major characteristics of NiV infection is the extensive infection and vasculitis of endothelial cells. NiV infects target cells by attaching to ephrin-B2 and -B3 receptors. These two receptors are highly expressed on endothelial cells, neurons, and smooth muscle cells [19]. The infection of endothelial cells by NiV leads to cell damage, formation of syncytium, and increased vascular permeability. Histopathological studies of both human and animal infections have shown vasculitis, thrombosis, and microinfarcts in various tissues and organs such as the lungs, spleen, and brain. The infection of endothelial cells by NiV leads to damage and results in increased vascular permeability [20]. This infection and damage of endothelial cells by NiV distinguish it as a neurotropic and vasculotropic virus (Fig. 3(3)). Neuroinvasion mechanisms Neurological involvement is a hallmark symptom in the clinical presentation of NiV infection, characterized by acute encephalitis with significant case fatality. Neuroinvasion is hypothesized to be mediated by hematogenous spread from endothelial cell infection and disruption of the BBB [20]. In addition, experimental data indicate that there is a potential mechanism for transneuronal spread via the olfactory route, providing a direct avenue from the nasal epithelium into the CNS [21]. Upon entry into the CNS, NiV infection causes inflammation, necrosis, and microvascular infarction in neurons and glial cells. Recurring or late-onset encephalitis in survivors may be attributed to viral persistence or immune-mediated neuropathology (Fig. 3(4)). Evidence from sequencing and strain diversity At the moment, many of the regions that experience outbreaks of the NiV do not have adequate genomic surveillance. This means that it is difficult to monitor the virus for any changes that might make it easier to transmit or more virulent. It is essential to sequence the genetic material of the virus on a regular basis because it enables scientists to monitor the evolution of the virus over time [4]. The integration of genomic surveillance with AI models could predict mutations that would affect transmissibility or antigenicity [22] (Fig. 3(5)). Risk of transmission from human to human Historical patterns Human-to-human transmission of the NiV has been observed mainly through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected persons, such as saliva, blood, urine, and respiratory fluids. This type of transmission has been most commonly observed in healthcare settings, where a lack of proper infection control practices can contribute to the spread of the virus among medical personnel and patients. In addition, human-to-human transmission of the virus has also been observed among family members and caregivers who provide direct care to infected patients in the home environment [23, 24] (Fig. 4). Reproductive number (R0) and efficiency Most of the studies on the outbreak of NiV have shown that the basic reproduction number (R0) is generally less than 1, which means that, on average, each infected individual will transmit the virus to fewer than one other person, and thus the chains of transmission will naturally die out. However, some cases, especially those involving respiratory symptoms such as coughing or difficulty breathing, have been shown to have a higher potential for transmission. In such cases, the virus can easily be transmitted to close contacts, healthcare workers, or caregivers, thereby increasing the risk of infection clusters [25] (Fig. 4). Impact of transmission mode If the respiratory system is involved in NiV infection, patients can generate virus-contaminated droplets and aerosols as a result of coughing or sneezing. This is particularly dangerous because it can easily spread the infection to people in close proximity, such as in a hospital setting. In this case, it is important to take infection control precautions to prevent the spread of the virus within a healthcare facility, such as wearing personal protective equipment (PPE) and isolating patients with the infection. Evaluation of the conditions under which NiV becomes more transmissible, such as co-infection, immune status of the host, or adaptations in the virus, would be important for predicting the risk of sustained human transmission [26] (Fig. 4). The pooled R0 value for EVD outbreaks has been found to be approximately 1.9, according to the results of several outbreaks, although there is a significant range depending on the setting and situation. The range in some countries has been from ~ 1.4 to > 3 in previous outbreaks [27]. In contrast, Nipah virus (NiV) has not been linked with human-to-human transmission during any outbreak, even though there is documented transmission of the virus among humans; however, such transmission is limited to close contacts only. Research findings and reports on Nipah virus transmission during outbreaks confirm that human-to-human transmission chains tend to be short, indicating that the R0 of Nipah virus is significantly less than 1 [5]. In contrast, SARS-CoV-2 transmissibility was much higher during the COVID-19 pandemic, with initial data on the emerging epidemic suggesting that the R0 of SARS-CoV-2 is significantly above 1, indicating rapid transmission of the virus across the globe. Although there is considerable variation depending on the variant, the emerging SARS-CoV-2 transmissibility during the pandemic is characterized by continued transmission across diverse populations worldwide [28]. Transmission efficiency The efficiency of transmission is affected by both shedding and route of transmission. SARS-CoV-2 is transmitted via respiratory droplets, which makes for efficient transmission between persons, thereby leading to epidemics. Asymptomatic persons also shed the virus at high levels, which makes for “hidden” transmission chains [28]. While the Ebola virus is capable of human-to-human transmission, its main mode of transmission is through direct contact with infectious body fluids, such as blood and vomit, and generally requires a level of close contact or caregiving environments, which limits its ability to spread in a community setting compared to other aerosol-transmitted diseases [27]. Similarly, transmission of NiV occurs mainly by direct contact with infected hosts or their secretions. Transmission of NiV among humans, as observed during outbreaks, has been attributed to close contact with infected individuals and their secretions, and not by efficient human-to-human transmission. Transmissions of NiV are rare, and transmission efficiency is low, as observed with other respiratory pathogens such as SARS-CoV-2 [5]. Airborne potential The airborne mode of transmission has a high potential for pandemic risks. This airborne potential has been responsible for the various super-spreading incidents reported during the COVID-19 pandemic [28]. full_text_sections.full_text: Abstract Nipah virus (NiV) is a highly pathogenic zoonotic RNA virus belonging to the genus Henipavirus within the family Paramyxoviridae, representing a continuing global health concern due to its high case fatality rate and potential for epidemic expansion in the era of increasing international connectivity. The virus demonstrates strong evolutionary adaptability driven by the absence of proofreading mechanisms during RNA replication, enabling genetic diversification that may influence host range, virulence, and transmission dynamics. Molecular pathogenesis of NiV is primarily mediated through interaction of viral glycoproteins with ephrin-B2 and ephrin-B3 receptors, facilitating host cell entry, endothelial damage, and neuroinvasion. Immune evasion facilitated by the action of accessory proteins encoded by the P gene (P, V, W, and C) acts to suppress innate antiviral immunity through the inhibition of interferon induction and JAK/STAT signaling. Human-to-human transmission of Nipah virus remains limited, with epidemiological evidence indicating basic reproduction numbers generally below unity; however, respiratory involvement and healthcare-associated exposure may enhance cluster outbreaks. Global travel, ecological disruption, and fragmented surveillance systems contribute to spillover risk, particularly in South and Southeast Asia where fruit bats of the genus Pteropus serve as natural reservoirs. Despite advances in vaccine technology, including subunit, viral vector, mRNA-based platforms, and monoclonal antibody therapies, no licensed prophylactic or therapeutic agent is currently available for human use. Global preparedness remains challenged by the scarcity of high-containment biosafety facilities, limited research funding, and absence of integrated One Health surveillance networks. Ethical considerations surrounding wildlife population control further complicate disease mitigation strategies. Emerging genomic surveillance, artificial intelligence–assisted predictive modeling, and regional data-sharing frameworks are essential for early detection and response. Strengthening molecular research on viral–host interactions and transmission determinants will be critical for preventing future Nipah virus outbreaks in an increasingly interconnected world. Graphical abstract Introduction Nipah virus (NiV) is an RNA virus that belongs to the family Paramyxoviridae. It is a member of the Henipavirus genus, which also comprises Hendra virus (HeV) and the newly discovered Cedar virus [1, 2]. NiV is a highly virulent Henipavirus that is mainly transmitted from fruit bats (of the genus Pteropus), its natural host, to humans either directly or through an intermediate host like pigs. NiV infections cause severe encephalitis and respiratory disease with case fatality rates ranging from 40 to 75% with no approved vaccines or antiviral therapies available [3]. The World Health Organization (WHO) has listed NiV as a priority pathogen because of its high mortality rate and potential for causing epidemics, and it recommends increased surveillance and preparedness [4]. Mutation potential RNA virus evolution Nipah virus (NiV), is an enveloped virus with a negative sense single-stranded RNA genome of helical symmetry. The nonsegmented, linear genome of Nipah virus is organized in the 3′ to 5′ direction and comprises six consecutively arranged genes that encode the nucleocapsid protein (N), phosphoprotein (P), matrix protein (M), fusion glycoprotein (F), attachment glycoprotein (G), and large polymerase (L) [5, 6] (Fig. 1). NiV being an RNA virus tends to have a higher rate of mutations compared to DNA viruses because RNA viruses do not have a proofreading mechanism during their replication. Because of the lack of proofreading ability during genome replication, the RNA virus NiV harbors evolutionary capacity. There is little information from genomic analysis supporting that natural mutation leads to any evolutionary change in either the range of host or its transmissibility or virulence in human cases. Hence, there is still a need for continued genome surveillance to look out for any such changes. The knowledge of this natural mutation ability is crucial in predicting the potential changes in the virulence, host range, and outbreak potential of the virus [7]. Genetic determinants of host interaction Attachment and entry mechanism The entry of NiV into host cells is mainly facilitated by its two surface glycoproteins, namely the G (attachment) glycoprotein and the F (fusion) glycoprotein. The G protein attaches with high affinity to the host cell surface receptors ephrin-B2 and ephrin-B3, which are highly conserved proteins among mammalian species. This attachment is crucial for the virus to attach to the host cell surface, and failure of the attachment process makes it impossible for the virus to enter the host cell. The conformational change that follows triggers the F glycoprotein to fuse the viral membrane with the host cell membrane, releasing the viral RNA into the cytoplasm for replication [8]. Structural basis and interactions Crystal structure analysis of the NiV-G glycoprotein in complex with ephrin-B2 or ephrin-B3 reveals that the viral protein interacts with the beta-propeller domain of these receptors through a defined protein–protein interface. This structural interaction defines the efficiency of viral attachment and infection. The shared binding interface for ephrin-B2 and ephrin-B3 enables NiV to infect a wide range of host cells, thus explaining the wide host tropism and high pathogenicity of NiV [9, 10]. Consequences of mutations on binding efficiency Mutational analysis and protein–protein interaction data suggest that certain residues within the host receptor and the viral glycoprotein can affect binding affinity and infection efficiency. For instance, mutations within the G-H loop of ephrin-B2 can modulate the binding affinity of NiV-G, thereby increasing or decreasing viral entry. Such modifications in binding efficiency can influence the viral infectivity and pathogenicity in various species [11]. Host tropism and computational predictions In silico analysis, such as protein–protein docking, has verified that NiV-G has stable interactions with ephrin-B2 and ephrin-B3 of various mammalian hosts, which implies that even small variations in the receptor sequences among species may affect host susceptibility. These models are valuable for predicting possible intermediate hosts and spillover susceptibility [12]. Therapeutic implications Given the importance of the G–ephrin interaction as an initial step in the NiV infection process, this interaction represents an attractive target for antiviral drugs and neutralizing antibodies. Inhibition of this interaction, either through the design of peptides that inhibit the binding of G to ephrin receptors or by locking the F protein in its prefusion state, could potentially inhibit viral entry and infection [13] (Fig. 2). These entry-associated mechanisms represent major targets for intervention and form the basis of several vaccine, monoclonal antibody, and antiviral strategies discussed in greater detail in the “Research Priorities” section of this review.
